A crosshair is a fine, thin line — or more commonly, a pair of two such lines crossing each other at their centers to form a "+" shape — used as a reference point for aiming, targeting, or aligning something precisely.

Think of it as a visual anchor. It tells your eye: "This exact center point is where your focus should be."

Picture the plus sign: +

Two straight lines — one running left to right (horizontal), one running top to bottom (vertical) — meet and cross at a single point in the middle. That meeting point, the dead center, is the most important part. It is what you align with whatever you are aiming at or measuring.

Sometimes the lines are solid all the way through. Sometimes there is a small gap or a dot at the center to make it even easier to pinpoint the exact spot.

Crosshairs appear in two broad worlds: the physical (real-life optical tools) and the digital (screens and software).

In physical/optical devices:

  • Rifle scopes and gun sights — A soldier or hunter looks through the scope and sees crosshairs. They align the center of the crosshairs with their target before firing. The crosshair tells them exactly where the bullet will land.
  • Telescopes — Astronomers use crosshairs inside telescope eyepieces to pinpoint the exact location of a star or planet.
  • Microscopes — Scientists use them to measure or mark a precise location on a specimen under the lens.
  • Surveying instruments — Engineers and land surveyors use crosshairs in their devices (like a theodolite) to take exact measurements of land and distances.
  • Camera viewfinders — Some cameras display crosshairs to help the photographer frame and focus a shot precisely.

In digital and virtual environments:

  • Video games — Almost every shooting game shows a crosshair on screen, overlaid on whatever the player's character is pointing their weapon at. It is your aiming guide in the virtual world.
  • Computer cursors — In image-editing software like Photoshop, or in technical drawing programs, the regular arrow cursor sometimes changes into a crosshair shape. This happens when pixel-perfect precision is needed — for example, when you are selecting an exact point on an image.
  • Graphical user interfaces (GUIs) — In software that deals with maps, charts, or precision design, a crosshair cursor helps the user click or interact with a very specific location.
What Is the Purpose of a Crosshair?

The purpose is always the same: precision.

Whenever a task requires you to identify, aim at, or align with an exact point — not roughly, not approximately, but exactly — a crosshair gives your eye a clear, unambiguous reference. Without it, you are guessing. With it, you have a precise guide.

Both the singular (crosshair) and plural (crosshairs) forms exist, and you will encounter both.

  • Crosshair (singular) technically refers to one of the individual lines.
  • Crosshairs (plural) refers to the full crossing pattern — both lines together as a single system.

In everyday usage, "crosshairs" (plural) is far more common, even when referring to the symbol as a whole. People rarely say "I put the crosshair on the target." They almost always say "I put the crosshairs on the target." The plural form has become the standard, natural way to refer to the entire thing.

Beyond its literal, physical meaning, "crosshairs" has a widely used figurative meaning in everyday language. This is possibly as common as its literal meaning, so you must know it.

To be in someone's crosshairs (or in the crosshairs) means to be the target of someone's focused attention, criticism, scrutiny, or hostility. It suggests that someone has "aimed" their full focus at you — usually with an intent that is threatening, aggressive, or at least intensely serious.

It comes directly from the idea of a shooter placing a target in the center of their rifle's crosshairs before pulling the trigger. To be in the crosshairs is to be in that dangerous, targeted position.

Examples of figurative use:

  • "After the financial scandal, the CEO found himself squarely in the crosshairs of government regulators."
    → Regulators were now intensely focused on him, investigating and targeting him.
  • "Small businesses have been in the crosshairs of rising inflation for months."
    → Inflation has been severely affecting and "targeting" small businesses.
  • "The rival company is in our crosshairs — we plan to compete directly with them this year."
    → The company has made the rival their specific, focused target.

The figurative use can imply anything from criticism and investigation to competition and rivalry to outright danger and threat, depending on the context. The core idea is always the same: someone or something has become a deliberate, focused target.

• "The sniper peered through his scope and placed the crosshairs on the distant target."
  • "In the video game, a red crosshair appeared on screen whenever the player aimed at an enemy."
  • "The cursor changed to a crosshair when she zoomed into the image to select a single pixel."
  • "The astronomer carefully adjusted the telescope until the star sat perfectly at the center of the crosshairs."

A crosshair is a "+" shaped marking used to pinpoint an exact location for aiming or precision, seen in scopes, games, and software — and in everyday language, to be "in the crosshairs" means to be someone's focused target.
